system_prompts.python:
You are an expert code generator specializing in data visualization. You will be given a request to generate code in a specific language and library. You MUST follow these rules:
1. Your response must contain ONLY raw, executable code for the requested language. Do not wrap it in markdown backticks (```), explanations, or any other text.
2. The code will be executed in a sandboxed, isolated Docker environment. You have access to standard python libraries such as pandas and numpy.
3. The environment has a pre-mounted data volume at '/app/data/'. All file I/O must use this path (e.g., read from '/app/data/input/' and write to '/app/data/output/').
4. Do NOT include any code that attempts to create directories, install packages, or perform any file system operations outside of the designated data paths.
5. Do NOT generate any harmful, malicious, or system-level code (e.g., using 'os' or 'subprocess'). If you are creating temporary files, let them be. Do not attempt to remove them. Such code will be rejected.

  • Columns:
    • organ_label (string) — e.g., “left breast”
    • as_label (string) — anatomical structure, e.g., “main lactiferous duct”, “mammary lobe”
    • cell_label (categorical, many levels) — e.g., “B cell”, “mast cell”
    • sex (categorical) — “Male”, “Female”
    • modality (string) — e.g., “sc_transcriptomics”
    • tool (string) — e.g., “popv”

  • Tooltips: organ_label, cell_label, count, pct (one decimal)

{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}

    {% else %}

6.initial_prompt:
You are an expert {{execution_env}} programmer. Generate complete, runnable {{execution_env}} code using {{library}} that:

Goal
- Loads a single-cell RNA-seq dataset and evaluates how filtering “promiscuous” genes (high mean expression across cells) affects clustering and UMAP visualization.
- Use exactly ONE threshold for now: THRESHOLDS = [1.0].

Inputs & Assumptions
- Input file path: `/app/data/input/dvl-llm-6-GTEx-immune-cells.h5ad`
- The dataset has:
  - adata.X: expression matrix (cells × genes)
  - adata.obs['granular']: cell type labels
- Output directory: /app/data/output/
- Use fixed random seeds where supported.

Environment-Specific Loading
{% if execution_env | lower == 'python' %}
  - Use Scanpy for loading and analysis:
    - Load with: sc.read_h5ad(`/app/data/input/dvl-llm-6-GTEx-immune-cells.h5ad`)
{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}
  - Use R native tools:
    - Load with: zellkonverter::readH5AD({{input_path}}) into SingleCellExperiment
    - Convert to Seurat if convenient; otherwise operate directly with SCE + uwot + igraph.
{% elif execution_env | lower == 'javascript' %}
  - JavaScript does not read .h5ad directly. Implement a thin pipeline that:
    - Invokes (or assumes output from) a Python preprocessing script to export two files for the single threshold T=1.0:
      1) embedding.csv with columns: UMAP1,UMAP2,leiden,granular,threshold
      2) metrics.json OR console print lines with ARI and NMI for T=1.0
    - Then load embedding.csv and render the two UMAP panels using {{library}}.
{% endif %}

Preprocessing (perform once before filtering)
- Normalize total counts per cell, then log1p transform.
{% if execution_env | lower == 'python' %}
  - Use: sc.pp.normalize_total(adata); sc.pp.log1p(adata)
{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}
  - Apply standard normalization (e.g., Seurat::NormalizeData with log-normalization) and log1p if needed.
{% elif execution_env | lower == 'javascript' %}
  - Preprocessing is done in the Python export step mentioned above.

Promiscuous Gene Identification (mean-based, on log1p scale)

- Build kNN graph (n_neighbors=15 or library default).
- Cluster with Leiden (or closest available community detection if Leiden is unavailable; note which was used).
- Compute UMAP embedding.
- Record the predicted cluster labels (call them “leiden”).

Metrics (per threshold)

{% if execution_env | lower == 'python' %}

{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}

{% endif %}
- Print exactly one console line:
  Threshold=<t>  ARI=<value>  NMI=<value>

Visualization (per threshold)
- Produce TWO UMAP plots for t=1.0:
  1) Left panel (or first file): color by “leiden”
  2) Right panel (or second file): color by “granular”
- Title each with: "UMAP — Threshold = <t>"
- Save to /app/data/output/{{filename_prefix}} with the correct extension by language/library:
Save the output visualization file to '/app/data/output/{{filename_prefix}}'.

You are an expert {{execution_env}} programmer. Generate {{execution_env}} code to read a dataset and produce a Sankey diagram using:

Programming language: {{execution_env}}
Library: {{library}}

Data profile:
    •   The dataset has these columns:

    •   donor_sex (categorical): Male, Female, Unknown.
    •   donor_bmi (numeric): 10–50.
    •   donor_race (categorical): mapped races like White, Black/African American, etc.
    •   organ_name (categorical): organ names of the samples.
    •   cell_type_annotation_tool (categorical): scRNA annotation tools.
    •   is_rui_registered (boolean string("true"/ "false")): whether RUI-registered.
    •   is_atlas_dataset (boolean string("true"/ "false")): whether part of an Atlas dataset.  

Required data transformations:
    1.  Read dataset:
    •   Read from '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-7-sankey.csv'.
    2. Replace missing/NA values in portal, donor_age, donor_sex, donor_bmi, donor_race, organ_name, cell_type_annotation_tool, is_rui_registered, is_atlas_dataset with descriptive placeholders (e.g., "Unknown Age", “Unknown Sex”, “Unknown Race”, "Unknown Organ").
    3.  Standardize portal names:
    •   Replace “HCA” and “CxG” with “CZ CELLxGENE”.
    •   Replace "NHLBI/LungMap" with "LungMap"
    •   Replace “HRA” with “HRA-OMAP”.
    4.  Standardize inconsistent donor_race values (“unknown”, “na”, “n/a” (and case variants) → "Unknown Race").
    5.  Standardize inconsistent donor_sex values (“unknown”, “na”, “n/a” (and case variants) → "Unknown Sex").
    6.  CT annotation tool replacement:
    •   Replace cell_type_annotation_tool values of “azimuth”, “celltypist” and “popv” with “sc_transcriptomics with Cell Summary”.

    •   Build nodes/links using unique value group counts.

Deliverable:
    •   Provide clean {{execution_env}} code in a single script to perform these transformations and generate the interactive Sankey diagram.

You are an expert {{ execution_env }} programmer.
Generate complete, runnable {{ execution_env }} code using {{ library }} to visualize distances from cells to their nearest endothelial cell for Healthy vs Diseased donors.

Input Data

Two donors: Healthy and Diseased. Each donor has:
  • Nodes CSV with columns: x, y, Cell Type.
  • Edges CSV with columns: Cell ID, Target ID, X1, Y1, Z1, X2, Y2, Z2.

  • Healthy: '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-healthy-nodes.csv', '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-healthy-edges.csv'
  • Diseased: '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-diseased-nodes.csv', '/app/data/input/dvl-llm-8-diseased-edges.csv'

  • Compute distance = sqrt((X1 - X2)^2 + (Y1 - Y2)^2) (ignore Z).
  • Join (X1, Y1) to nodes (x, y) to fetch Cell Type. Use a rounded coordinate key if exact matches fail (e.g., round to 1 decimal).
  • Produce tidy columns: cell_type, distance_um, tissue_type ∈ {"Healthy","Diseased"}.

      - Ensure y-axis starts at 0: `coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, NA))`
      - Include all cell types on the x-axis (union of both donors); rotate labels ~20–30°.
      {% endif %}

Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% endif %}\n{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}\n    {% if library | lower == 'plotly' %}\n        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n  {% elif library | lower == 'ggdist' %} Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/` using `ggsave("{{ filename_prefix }}.png", plot, width = 12, height = 6, dpi = 300)`.  {% else %}\n        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.\n    {% endif %}\n {% else %} Save the visualization as a `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`. {% endif %}

9.initial_prompt:
You are an expert data engineer and visualization developer.
Generate {{execution_env}} code that reads two CSVs and writes one visualization file implementing the spec below. Do not ask for input; hard-code paths. Use deterministic randomness.

Use
	•	PROGRAMMING_ENV = {{execution_env}}
	•	VIZ_LIBRARY     = {{library}}

⸻
Inputs (read from working directory)
	•	/app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-nodes.csv with columns: x, y, Cell Type
	•	/app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-edges.csv with columns: Cell ID, Target ID, (optional X1..Z2)

Identity rule:
	•	After loading and cleaning dvl-llm-9-cde-nodes.csv, create cell_id = np.arange(N) and use it as the ONLY identifier everywhere.
	•	Never rely on DataFrame.index for identity.
	•	Never compute medians or choices from DataFrame.index. Operate on sorted cell_id arrays.

Assumptions:
	•	Coordinates are 2D (x, y); drop non-finite rows.
	•	Standardize cell type labels by trimming whitespace; treat case-insensitively when counting.

Output (exactly one file):
	Save the output visualization file to '/app/data/output/{{filename_prefix}}'. {% if execution_env | lower == 'python' %}
    {% if library | lower in ['plotly', 'altair', 'pygal', 'bokeh'] %}
        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.
    {% elif library | lower in ['matplotlib', 'seaborn', 'plotnine'] %}
        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.
    {% endif %}
{% elif execution_env | lower == 'r' %}
    {% if library | lower in ['plotly', 'echarts', 'apache echarts', 'highcharter', 'ggiraph'] %}
        Save the visualization as an `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`.
    {% else %}
        Save the visualization as a `.png` file to `/app/data/output/`.
    {% endif %}
 {% else %} Save the visualization as a `.html` file to `/app/data/output/`. {% endif %}

⸻

Deterministic configuration (use these defaults; make constants at the top)
RANDOM_STATE = 42

# Seeding for Level-0 (to keep 420k rows tractable)
MAX_SEEDS  = 1500
GRID_CELLS = 40
PER_BIN    = 1          # seeds per non-empty grid bin (can be >1)

# Neighborhood construction (radius in same units as x,y)
DISTANCE_MAX = 265.0
K_NEIGHBORS  = 30       # cap per seed within the radius

# Multi-seed grouping (break the 1:1 seed↔neighborhood)
SEED_CLUSTER_EPS          = DISTANCE_MAX   # DBSCAN eps on seed coordinates
SEED_CLUSTER_MIN_SAMPLES  = 1

# Community clustering
N_CLUSTERS = 12

# Region mapping via keywords (domain-guided)
REGION_KEYWORDS = {
  "Mucosa":   ["epithelial","goblet","secretory","tumor"],
  "Muscle":   ["smooth muscle","myocyte","myofibroblast","muscle","muscle/fibroblast"],
  "Submucosa":["fibroblast","endothelial","immune","macrophage","lymphocyte",
               "b cell","t cell","tc cell","t helper","treg","stromal"]
}

# Block-stacked layout columns (x positions)
X_COLS = {"cell":0.0, "nh":1.0, "comm":2.0, "region":3.0}

Required pipeline (implement exactly)
	1.	Load & clean
		•	Read /app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-nodes.csv, standardize to columns: x, y, cell_type (trim; case-insensitive for counting). Drop non-finite x,y.
		•	Create a new column cell_id as consecutive integers from 0 to N-1, where N is the number of rows. This cell_id is the only identifier used for all later steps.
		•	/app/data/input/dvl-llm-9-cde-edges.csv (optional): keep only Cell ID, Target ID. Canonicalize undirected (a<b), drop self-loops/dupes. Do not use edges in this version for clustering—just load for possible QC.
	2.	Select seeds (Level-0)
		•	Compute the minimum and maximum of the x and y coordinates. If the minimum equals the maximum for either axis, artificially expand that range slightly to avoid zero-width bins.
		•	Divide the coordinate space into a grid of GRID_CELLS × GRID_CELLS.
		•	Assign each cell into exactly one bin on this grid. Make sure that cells lying exactly on the maximum boundaries are assigned into the last bin rather than excluded.
		•	For each non-empty bin, collect all cell_id values of the cells in that bin and sort them. From this sorted list, select up to PER_BIN representative cells. These representatives must be chosen deterministically by selecting IDs centered around the median of the list.
		•	Combine the representatives from all bins. Remove duplicates. Sort the combined list by cell_id.
		•	If the total number of seeds exceeds MAX_SEEDS, reduce the list deterministically by evenly spaced sampling across the sorted list. Do not use randomness at this stage.
		•	The final result is the ordered list of seed_ids.
	3.	Spatial index construction: 
		•	Build a data structure that can query the nearest neighbors of any point based on Euclidean distance. This will be used to find nearby cells for each seed.
	4.	Multi-seed neighborhoods
		•	Cluster the spatial positions of the seeds using DBSCAN with parameters: radius equal to SEED_CLUSTER_EPS and minimum samples equal to SEED_CLUSTER_MIN_SAMPLES.
		•	Each DBSCAN cluster of seeds defines exactly one neighborhood. If DBSCAN labels any seed as noise (label = -1), treat that seed as its own single-seed neighborhood.
		•	For each seed in a cluster:
		•	Query all neighbors within DISTANCE_MAX using the spatial index.
		•	Sort the neighbors by distance from the seed.
		•	Exclude the seed itself.
		•	Retain only the first K_NEIGHBORS neighbors, even if more are available within the radius.
		•	Always include the seed itself in the neighborhood.
		•	Combine all members (seeds and their neighbors) of a cluster to form the final membership list for that neighborhood. Remove duplicates within a neighborhood.
		•	For each neighborhood, compute metadata:
		•	A sequential neighborhood_id.
		•	The number of seeds in the neighborhood.
		•	The list of seed IDs included.
		•	The size, defined as the number of unique member cells.
		•	The centroid, defined as the mean of x and y coordinates of its members.
		•	The dominant cell type, defined as the most frequent type among its members, case-insensitive.
	5.	Community clustering from neighborhoods
		•	Construct a global list of all unique cell types across the dataset, standardized to lower case, and sort this list to fix a consistent order.
		•	Build a matrix with one row per neighborhood and one column per cell type. Each entry is the count of how many members of that neighborhood belong to that cell type.
		•	Apply KMeans clustering to this matrix with number of clusters equal to the minimum of N_CLUSTERS and the number of neighborhoods. Set the random state deterministically.
		•	Assign each neighborhood a community_id.
		•	For each community, compute metadata:
		•	The number of neighborhoods it contains.
		•	The centroid, defined as the mean of the centroids of its neighborhoods.
	6.	Region assignment (functional tissue units)
		•	Define three main region categories with their keyword lists: Mucosa, Muscle, Submucosa.
		•	For each cell type label, determine if it matches any region’s keywords using case-insensitive substring matching.
		•	For each community, collect the dominant cell types of its neighborhoods, map these to regions, and determine the majority region by vote.
		•	If no clear region can be determined, fall back to using the community’s dominant cell type as the region label.
	7.	Layout for visualization
		•	Use fixed x-coordinates for each hierarchy level: cells at 0.0, neighborhoods at 1.0, communities at 2.0, regions at 3.0.
		•	Order the seeds by the tuple (region, community, descending neighborhood size, cell_id).
		•	Assign y-coordinates sequentially to seeds in this order.
		•	Assign each neighborhood the y-coordinate of its first seed in this ordering.
		•	Assign each community the average y-coordinate of its neighborhoods.
		•	Assign each region the average y-coordinate of its communities.
		•	Do not display axes or gridlines for the y-axis.
	8.	Styling of visualization
		•	Symbols: cells as circles, neighborhoods as squares, communities as upward triangles, regions as diamonds.
		•	Colors:
		•	Cells and neighborhoods colored by cell type (neighborhood uses its dominant type).
		•	Communities and regions colored by region assignment.
		•	Edges:
		•	Cell to neighborhood edges drawn thin.
		•	Neighborhood to community edges drawn medium thickness.
		•	Community to region edges drawn thick.
	9.	Constraints
		•	Script must run end-to-end as is. Set random seeds for determinism.

Use n_clusters=10, random_state=123 for KMeans.
Place columns: Cell(0)→NH(1)→Comm(2)→Region(3).
Set --hide-cell-edges true (or filter edges).
Set background color to white
